name: Time Series Benchmark Suite (TSBS)
summary: A Go toolkit that generates synthetic server-monitoring or IoT time series, bulk-loads it into a database and times a fixed set of time-series queries.
intro: TSBS is a set of Go programs. You pick a use case, a random seed, a scale (how many hosts or trucks), a time range and a reading interval, and `tsbs_generate_data` writes the data in the target database’s own load format. `devops` simulates 9 groups of server metrics, 100 values per host per reading; `cpu-only` keeps just 10 CPU metrics; `iot` simulates a fleet of trucks, with out-of-order and missing readings and late batches from trucks that were offline. The same seed gives every database identical data and identical queries. 4,000 hosts over three days at 10-second intervals is just over 100 million rows (1 billion metrics).

A run has three phases. First, data and queries are generated ahead of time, so generating them doesn’t slow the measurement. Second, `tsbs_load` (or a per-database `tsbs_load_<db>`) inserts the file with a chosen number of workers and batch size and reports metrics per second and rows per second. Third, `tsbs_run_queries_<db>` replays a file of one query type with N workers and reports minimum, median, mean, maximum and standard deviation of latency, plus wall-clock time. There are 15 devops query types (for example the max of one metric for 1 host over 1 hour, or the last reading of every host) and 12 IoT ones (last location, low fuel, driving sessions).

There is no official results page. Whoever wants numbers runs it on their own hardware with their own settings, and in practice that is usually a database vendor. The upstream repository has no releases or tags, and its last code change was in September 2023.

caveats: Vendors wrote it. InfluxData built the original to publish comparisons such as “InfluxDB is 27x Faster vs MongoDB for Time-Series Workloads”. Timescale forked it in 2018 and used it in its own posts. The data shape and query list follow the monitoring and IoT workloads those products target.

The data is synthetic: the generator inherited from influxdb-comparisons emits random walks per host at a fixed interval. Value distributions and regularity drive compression and query cost, so real data can behave quite differently.

Upstream code is old. It supports InfluxDB 1.x only; a pull request for InfluxDB 2.x has been open since July 2025, and InfluxDB 3 needs its own support (QuestDB’s fork added it). Tiger Data’s own TimescaleDB vs InfluxDB post compared TimescaleDB 1.7.1 with InfluxDB 1.8.0. Check the version and date behind any number you see.

Vendors keep their own forks. QuestDB’s fork adds loader optimisations for QuestDB, its own binary protocol and InfluxDB 2 and 3 support; TDengine and GreptimeDB keep copies too. Numbers produced by different forks aren’t comparable.

The results you find are vendor-run. QuestDB’s README, for example, shows QuestDB loading 8.59 million rows per second against 1.75 million for ClickHouse and 1.08 million for TimescaleDB on one r8a.8xlarge, all run by QuestDB in August 2026. Worker count, batch size and each database’s tuning flags (chunk size, partitioning, indexes) move such numbers a lot.

Loading and querying are measured separately; the README says concurrent inserts and queries aren’t tested, though that is how most monitoring systems run. The query set is mostly time-bucketed aggregates, threshold filters and last-point lookups.

items.name: influxdb-comparisons
items.text: The original suite TSBS was forked from, focused on the devops use case. It still gets dependency updates.

items.name: questdb/tsbs
items.text: Actively maintained fork with QuestDB loader optimisations, its binary QWP protocol, query-generation fixes and InfluxDB 2 and 3 support.

items.name: taosdata/tsbs and GreptimeTeam/tsbs
items.text: TDengine’s copy adds a TDengine target for devops and IoT; GreptimeDB keeps a fork of the upstream repository.

items.name: SciTS
items.text: Independent benchmark from a 2022 paper for scientific and industrial IoT workloads; tests inserts, queries and resource use on TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, PostgreSQL and ClickHouse.

items.name: ClickBench
items.text: Not a time-series benchmark: 43 analytical queries over one web-analytics table, with a public results page that time-series databases also appear on.
